# Road Bike

## Overview

I picked up a used aluminium frame in size 56 last spring and rebuilt it around a Shimano 105 groupset. The wheels are hand-built 32-hole rims on sealed hubs, and I run 28 mm tyres, usually at the pressures noted below. Total mass sits around 9.2 kg with pedals and two bottle cages. It is nothing exotic, but it does the job for 60 to 120 km outings and the odd wet commute. The paint has a few chips on the top tube from leaning it against things.

## Setup

Saddle height started from the heel-on-pedal method and ended up 74.5 cm from the bottom bracket centre. Reach is a 100 mm stem with 420 mm bars, wrapped in 3 mm tape. Cleats are set so my knees track straight; I moved the left cleat 2 mm forward to quiet a hot spot on longer days. Gearing is 50/34 up front and 11-32 at the back, which covers most of the hills near home. I run tubes rather than tubeless because I hate topping up sealant.

## Maintenance

Every 500 km I drop the chain wear gauge in and replace the chain once it hits 0.5% elongation. Tyre pressure goes to 90 psi front and 95 psi rear before each outing, checked with a decent floor pump. I grab the fork and frame, then rock them to feel for headset bearing play and tighten the preload cap if there is any movement. Brake pad wear gets a look every couple of weeks, and I swap pads once the wear line disappears. The cassette lockring torques to 40 Nm, and I wipe the drivetrain down with a rag and re-lube after wet weather.

## Troubleshooting

A creak under load usually traces to the seatpost or the chainring bolts; grease both and it goes away. If shifting hesitates on the way up the cassette, the cable has stretched and needs a quarter turn of barrel adjustment. Brake rub after a wheel swap is almost always a slightly bent rotor, which I true by hand with a small spanner. A soft front brake lever means a bubble in the hose, so I bleed it and top up the mineral oil. Worn cleats cause a float that feels vague; replacing them fixes the noise.
